message.content:
# Investigative Report: 2023 3CX DesktopApp Software Supply-Chain Compromise

## Executive assessment

The public evidence supports a specific, two-stage supply-chain compromise. The 3CX incident was not initiated solely by tampering with the 3CX DesktopApp distribution process. According to Mandiant’s investigation, the intrusion into 3CX began when a 3CX employee downloaded and installed a maliciously modified version of Trading Technologies’ X_TRADER software. That earlier compromise gave the attackers access to the 3CX environment. The attackers then moved laterally, harvested credentials, compromised both Windows and macOS build environments, and inserted malicious code into legitimate 3CX DesktopApp installers. Those trojanized installers were distributed to 3CX customers in March 2023. Mandiant characterized this as the first confirmed case in which one software-supply-chain compromise directly enabled another software-supply-chain compromise ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)).

The public attribution is best expressed as a suspected North Korean nexus, with the activity tracked by Mandiant as **UNC4736**. Kaspersky attributed the Gopuram-related activity to **Lazarus** with medium-to-high confidence, while MITRE ATT&CK identifies Lazarus Group as a North Korean state-sponsored group and associates it with AppleJeus. CrowdStrike reporting cited by Cybersecurity Dive associated the incident with **Labyrinth Chollima**, an alias associated with Lazarus Group in MITRE’s knowledge base. However, public reporting did not establish with absolute certainty that every actor or operational cluster associated with the wider North Korean cyber ecosystem was identical. The most defensible conclusion is therefore: **UNC4736 was a suspected North Korean activity cluster, assessed by Mandiant as related to financially motivated AppleJeus activity and overlapping with Lazarus-linked tradecraft; Kaspersky separately assessed the Gopuram deployment as likely Lazarus activity** ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise); [S2](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/); [S3](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032/)).

## Scope and source basis

This report reconstructs the public evidence chain using the supplied benchmark sources. The principal evidentiary source is Mandiant’s April 20, 2023 technical investigation, because it directly addresses the initial intrusion vector, movement through 3CX, compromise of build systems, malware components, and attribution. Kaspersky’s contemporaneous reporting provides independent evidence regarding the targeted deployment of Gopuram and the apparent focus on cryptocurrency companies. Google Threat Analysis Group reporting from March 2022 supplies historical context concerning the compromise of Trading Technologies’ website and North Korean AppleJeus activity directed at cryptocurrency and fintech organizations. Government guidance from Singapore’s Cyber Security Agency corroborates the affected application versions and the customer-facing risk.

The supplied material contains duplicate copies of several sources. Each unique source is assigned one source identifier:

| Source ID | Source | Primary evidentiary value |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | Mandiant/Google Cloud, April 20, 2023 | Initial access, propagation, build-environment compromise, UNC4736 assessment |
| S2 | Kaspersky Securelist, April 3, 2023 | Gopuram deployment, victim selectivity, Lazarus assessment |
| S3 | MITRE ATT&CK Lazarus Group | Group identity, aliases, associated malware and techniques |
| S4 | MITRE ATT&CK AppleJeus | AppleJeus relationship to Lazarus and cryptocurrency targeting |
| S5 | Google TAG, March 24, 2022 | Earlier Trading Technologies compromise and AppleJeus context |
| S6 | Cybersecurity Dive, March 30, 2023 | Scale, affected customer ecosystem, initial public reporting |
| S7 | Cyber Security Agency of Singapore, March 31, 2023 | Affected 3CX versions and defensive guidance |
| S8 | WIRED, April 3, 2023 | Early evidence of surgical cryptocurrency targeting |
| S9 | WIRED, April 20, 2023 | Public explanation of the cascading supply-chain compromise |

## Reconstruction of the evidence chain

### 1. Earlier compromise of Trading Technologies infrastructure

The earliest publicly described element in the chain was not the 3CX build system. Mandiant identified a malware-laced installer for **X_TRADER**, a Trading Technologies software package, as the initial compromise vector into 3CX. The affected installer was identified as `X_TRADER_r7.17.90p608.exe`, with MD5 hash `ef4ab22e565684424b4142b1294f1f4d`. Mandiant reported that the installer remained available for download from the legitimate Trading Technologies website in 2022, even though the X_TRADER platform had reportedly been discontinued in 2020 ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)).

Mandiant’s technical analysis found that the modified X_TRADER installer was signed with a certificate whose subject was “Trading Technologies International, Inc.” The installer executed a signed `Setup.exe`, which dropped malicious DLLs and a benign executable. The benign executable was used to side-load a malicious DLL. The loaded components used **SIGFLIP** and **DAVESHELL** to decrypt and load a modular backdoor named **VEILEDSIGNAL** into memory. VEILEDSIGNAL could send implant information, execute shellcode, and terminate itself. Its associated modules supported process injection and encrypted command-and-control communications ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)).

Google TAG had previously reported that the legitimate `www.tradingtechnologies.com` website was compromised in February 2022 and hosted a hidden iframe associated with a Chrome exploitation campaign. TAG attributed the campaign to activity publicly tracked as **Operation AppleJeus**, which targeted cryptocurrency and fintech users. TAG observed that the attackers compromised legitimate fintech websites and used hidden iframes to deliver an exploit kit, including activity directed at visitors to Trading Technologies ([S5](https://blog.google/threat-analysis-group/countering-threats-north-korea/)). This earlier evidence does not, by itself, prove that the same exact intrusion altered the X_TRADER installer or that the 3CX compromise began in February 2022. It does, however, establish a documented North Korean-linked compromise of Trading Technologies infrastructure preceding the later X_TRADER distribution described by Mandiant.

### 2. Installation of the malicious X_TRADER package on a 3CX employee’s computer

Mandiant determined that a 3CX employee’s computer had been compromised after the employee installed the malicious X_TRADER software. This provided the attackers with an initial foothold inside the 3CX corporate environment. The evidence does not establish that 3CX was a customer of Trading Technologies or that X_TRADER was officially required for 3CX operations. In fact, Trading Technologies reportedly stated that X_TRADER was a trading-professional tool and that there was no obvious reason for it to have been installed on a 3CX machine ([S9](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-times-two)).

That uncertainty is important. The evidence establishes the technical pathway—malicious X_TRADER software was present on a 3CX employee’s system—but it does not publicly establish why the employee installed it, whether the installation was authorized, or how the attackers initially compromised the Trading Technologies software package. Mandiant explicitly stated that it had not been hired by Trading Technologies to investigate the original X_TRADER compromise and therefore could not determine how the application had been modified or how many other victims might have been affected ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)).

### 3. Lateral movement and compromise of the 3CX build environment

After obtaining access through the employee’s computer, the attackers moved through the 3CX environment. Mandiant reported that the attackers harvested credentials and moved laterally until they compromised both the Windows and macOS build environments. The attackers used a compiled version of the open-source **Fast Reverse Proxy** project to move laterally within the 3CX organization. A file named `MsMpEng.exe`, with MD5 `19dbffec4e359a198daf4ffca1ab9165`, was dropped into `C:\Windows\System32` ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)).

On the Windows build environment, the attackers deployed the **TAXHAUL** launcher and **COLDCAT** downloader. TAXHAUL persisted by exploiting DLL search-order hijacking through the IKEEXT service and ran with LocalSystem privileges. COLDCAT generated host identifiers and communicated with a configured command-and-control server, receiving shellcode after an initial handshake ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)).

The macOS build server was compromised with **POOLRAT**, which used Launch Daemons for persistence. Mandiant corrected earlier reporting that had referred to a different malware family, stating that analysis identified the macOS backdoor as POOLRAT rather than a new family called SIMPLESEA ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)).

The build-environment compromise was the critical bridge between the first and second supply-chain attacks. Once the attackers controlled the build infrastructure, they could modify legitimate 3CX application components and distribute malicious versions to customers while preserving the appearance of a normal vendor update.

### 4. Trojanization and distribution of the 3CX DesktopApp

The malicious 3CX package was distributed through legitimate 3CX DesktopApp installers. The affected software included 3CX DesktopApp version **18.12.416 and earlier**, according to Mandiant. The malicious code ran a downloader called **SUDDENICON**, which retrieved additional command-and-control server information from encrypted icon files hosted in a GitHub repository. A subsequent payload, identified as **ICONICSTEALER**, collected browser information and other application data ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)).

Kaspersky described the infection chain in similar terms. The malicious MSI installers contained an infected DLL that decrypted shellcode from the overlay of `d3dcompiler_47.dll`. The decrypted payload extracted command-and-control URLs from icons in a GitHub repository. It then connected to a command-and-control server, downloaded an information stealer, and collected system information and browser history ([S2](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/)).

The customer impact was potentially broad because 3CX was widely deployed. Cybersecurity Dive reported vendor claims of more than **600,000 corporate customers** and more than **12 million active daily users**. Huntress reportedly identified more than **242,000 publicly exposed 3CX phone-management systems** and sent 2,595 incident reports involving a maliciously signed `3CXDesktopApp.exe` binary ([S6](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/)). These figures describe potential exposure and observed indicators, not confirmed compromise of every customer.

The Cyber Security Agency of Singapore identified affected Windows Electron versions **18.12.407 and 18.12.416**, and affected macOS Electron versions **18.11.1213, 18.12.402, 18.12.407, and 18.12.416**. It advised users and administrators to uninstall affected software, conduct full antivirus scans, search for indicators of compromise, and block associated domains ([S7](https://www.csa.gov.sg/alerts-and-advisories/alerts/al-2023-040/)).

## Targeting and operational objectives

### Broad initial reach, narrow follow-on targeting

The evidence indicates a distinction between the large number of systems that may have received the malicious 3CX software and the much smaller number that received or executed the more capable second-stage payloads. Kaspersky observed Gopuram on fewer than ten infected machines in its telemetry and described the deployment as highly selective. The identified victims included cryptocurrency companies, with observed infections concentrated in several countries, including Brazil, Germany, Italy, and France ([S2](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/)).

WIRED reported that Kaspersky identified a small number of cryptocurrency-focused firms in western Asia among the victims. Gopuram was described as a final-stage backdoor capable of interacting with the victim’s file system and creating processes. Kaspersky did not report evidence of actual cryptocurrency theft in the cases it observed, so the financial objective remains an assessment rather than a demonstrated outcome ([S8](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-north-korea-cryptocurrency-targets/)).

The observed pattern is consistent with a reconnaissance-and-filtering model: a trusted application provides broad access, the attacker collects information about infected systems, and only selected victims receive a more capable implant. This interpretation is supported by the sequence of SUDDENICON, ICONICSTEALER, and Gopuram described by Mandiant and Kaspersky, but the public record does not establish the complete victim set or every operational objective ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise); [S2](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/)).

### Gopuram and AppleJeus relationships

Kaspersky found Gopuram coexisting with AppleJeus during an earlier investigation of a Southeast Asian cryptocurrency company. It also identified infrastructure overlap between a Gopuram-related sample and infrastructure previously associated with AppleJeus, including `wirexpro[.]com`. Kaspersky further observed a related malicious MSI sample whose in-memory payload contacted `oilycargo[.]com`, a domain previously attributed by multiple researchers to Lazarus ([S2](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/)).

Mandiant similarly assessed with moderate confidence that UNC4736 was related to financially motivated North Korean AppleJeus activity. Mandiant cited shared code and loading characteristics, including the same RC4 key, use of SIGFLIP and DAVESHELL, the hard-coded `__tutma` cookie variable, and AES-256-GCM encryption. It also linked POOLRAT in the 3CX environment to an older POOLRAT sample previously reported in the AppleJeus operation involving CoinGoTrade ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)).

MITRE ATT&CK describes AppleJeus as a downloader family initially embedded in trojanized cryptocurrency applications and identifies Lazarus Group as its associated group. It also describes Lazarus as a North Korean state-sponsored group attributed to the Reconnaissance General Bureau, while cautioning that public reporting often uses “Lazarus Group” as an umbrella term for multiple North Korean operators ([S4](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0584/); [S3](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032/)).

## Attribution assessment

### Primary public cluster designation

Mandiant tracked the 3CX activity as **UNC4736**, a suspected North Korean nexus cluster. Mandiant assessed with moderate confidence that UNC4736 was related to financially motivated North Korean AppleJeus activity. The assessment was based on malware, infrastructure, targeting, and code similarities rather than on a publicly identified perpetrator or direct admission ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise)).

Kaspersky attributed the Gopuram deployment to **Lazarus** with medium-to-high confidence. Its reasoning relied on Gopuram’s prior coexistence with AppleJeus, shared infrastructure, similarities in loader shellcode, and domains associated with Lazarus activity. Kaspersky also acknowledged that some shellcode was based on open-source code used by other threat actors, meaning that individual technical similarities were not independently conclusive ([S2](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/)).

Cybersecurity Dive reported that CrowdStrike connected the campaign to **Labyrinth Chollima**, a North Korea-linked threat actor active since at least 2009 ([S6](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/)). MITRE lists Labyrinth Chollima as an associated group name under Lazarus Group, although alias relationships should not be treated as proof that every operation attributed to one label was conducted by a single organizational unit ([S3](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032/)).

### Attribution conclusion

The strongest evidence-based conclusion is that the 3CX compromise was conducted by a **North Korea-linked, financially motivated activity cluster publicly tracked by Mandiant as UNC4736**, with substantial public reporting connecting parts of the operation—especially Gopuram and AppleJeus-related infrastructure—to Lazarus Group. The evidence supports a Lazarus/AppleJeus relationship, but the appropriate confidence level remains qualified because Mandiant used “suspected” and “moderate confidence,” Kaspersky’s conclusion concerned the Gopuram deployment, and North Korean operations frequently share infrastructure, malware, and personnel.

## Contradictions and limitations

The supplied sources contain several differences in terminology and confidence:

1. **UNC4736 versus Lazarus versus Labyrinth Chollima.** Mandiant used UNC4736, Kaspersky used Lazarus, and CrowdStrike reporting used Labyrinth Chollima. These labels may describe overlapping activity, but the sources do not provide a single universally accepted organizational identity ([S1](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/3cx-software-supply-chain-compromise); [S2](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/); [S3](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032/)).

2. **Kimsuky, Emerald Sleet, and Velvet Chollima in early WIRED reporting.** The April 20 WIRED article used these names when describing the suspected North Korean group, whereas Mandiant’s own technical report tracked the activity as UNC4736. The supplied evidence does not independently resolve whether the WIRED labels identify the same operational cluster or reflect broader naming differences ([S9](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-times-two/)).

3. **Actual theft was not demonstrated.** The sources support a cryptocurrency-related targeting hypothesis, but Kaspersky reported no observed evidence of cryptocurrency theft in the cases it examined. Therefore, cryptocurrency theft should be described as a likely or assessed objective, not a confirmed impact ([S2](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/); [S8](https://www.wired.com/story/3cx-supply-chain-attack-north-korea-cryptocurrency-targets/)).

4. **Victim counts are not equivalent.** The 600,000-customer figure represents the vendor’s customer base; 242,000 represents publicly exposed systems identified by Huntress; and fewer than ten represents Kaspersky-observed Gopuram deployments. These are different populations and must not be combined into a single confirmed infection count ([S2](https://securelist.com/gopuram-backdoor-deployed-through-3cx-supply-chain-attack/109344/); [S6](https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/news/supply-chain-attack-3cx-desktop-thousands/646432/)).

## Final findings

- The 3CX compromise was initiated through an earlier compromise involving a trojanized Trading Technologies X_TRADER installer.
- A 3CX employee installed the malicious X_TRADER software, creating the initial foothold in the 3CX environment.
- The attackers harvested credentials and moved laterally within 3CX.
- Both Windows and macOS build environments were compromised.
- The attackers used TAXHAUL, COLDCAT, POOLRAT, and related tooling during the build-environment intrusion.
- Malicious code was inserted into legitimate 3CX DesktopApp installers.
- The trojanized application distributed SUDDENICON and, in later stages, ICONICSTEALER.
- Gopuram was deployed selectively against a small number of high-value victims, especially cryptocurrency-related organizations.
- The primary Mandiant designation was UNC4736, a suspected North Korean nexus cluster.
- Kaspersky assessed the Gopuram-related activity as likely Lazarus, while MITRE associates AppleJeus with Lazarus Group.
- The public evidence supports a financially motivated North Korean connection but does not prove that cryptocurrency theft occurred in every—or any specifically identified—victim environment.
